analysis.one_liner: Guarantees Medicare beneficiaries can buy supplemental insurance without health-based denials or price discrimination.
analysis.headline: The Medigap Portability Act was introduced with bipartisan sponsorship in September 1996, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received any action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required insurers selling Medicare supplement (Medigap) policies to sell coverage to people who lost their coverage through no fault of their own — because an HMO left their area, an insurer went bankrupt, or a retiree plan shut down — without denying them, charging them more, or excluding their pre-existing conditions. It also would have banned pre-existing-condition exclusions during the initial six-month Medigap enrollment period and extended that enrollment window to disabled Medicare beneficiaries under 65. It would have funded consumer information programs to help beneficiaries compare plans, paid for by assessments on the insurers themselves.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries whose coverage falls apart through no fault of their own: people whose Medicare HMO leaves the area or shuts down, whose Medigap insurer goes bankrupt or stops selling new policies, or whose employer retiree plan ends. Also disabled beneficiaries under 65, who currently lack a guaranteed six-month window to buy a Medigap policy without health screening.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries losing coverage, especially the disabled

how_it_helps.text: Requires Medigap issuers to guarantee issue — with no denial, no health-based pricing, and no pre-existing-condition exclusions — to people who lost HMO, Medigap, or retiree supplemental coverage due to plan exits, insurer insolvency, or a move, if they apply within 63 days [S2, S3]
Bars insurers from excluding benefits for pre-existing conditions during the initial six-month Medigap enrollment period after a person first becomes eligible for Medicare [S2, S3]
Extends the six-month initial Medigap enrollment window to non-elderly Medicare beneficiaries, including those who become eligible through disability [S2, S3]

Authorizes grants to nonprofit consumer organizations and state agencies to give Medicare beneficiaries clear, standardized comparisons of Medigap policies and Medicare managed care plans, including required consumer satisfaction survey results [S2, S3]

analysis.who_pays: Medigap insurers and Medicare managed care plans. They must accept applicants regardless of health status at standard prices, conduct consumer satisfaction surveys, and pay assessments — capped at $35 million per year — to fund the consumer information grant program. These costs are likely to be passed into premiums.

drawbacks.text: Guaranteed issue without health-based pricing can raise premiums for healthier enrollees, since insurers spread the cost of covering sicker applicants across the whole pool [S2, S3]
The guarantee is limited: it applies to people losing coverage for specified reasons, and the new policy they are offered can have benefits 'comparable or lesser' than what they had [S3]
The consumer information program is funded by assessments on insurers and plans of up to $35 million per year, a cost that could be reflected in premiums [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are targeted at a genuine gap: before this era, a Medicare beneficiary whose private coverage collapsed could find Medigap policies unaffordable or unavailable because of their health. The costs — broader risk pools and modest assessments — fall on the insurance industry and are partly passed into premiums. The bill's narrow trigger conditions and the allowance for lesser-benefit policies temper its reach, but on balance the protections are real and the costs are modest and spread widely.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and Congress adjourned in January 1997 with the bill dead.

narrative.text: Sen. John Chafee, joined by Sen. John Rockefeller, introduced the Medigap Portability Act of 1996 in the Senate on September 16, 1996 [S3, S5]
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day — the only committee action it received [S5]
It drew three cosponsors — one Democrat and two Republicans — in addition to its Republican sponsor [S4]
No further action appears in the record, and the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, leaving the bill to die in committee [S5, S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medigap insurers and Medicare managed care plans are better off: they never had to accept applicants regardless of health, price without health screening, or pay the assessments for consumer information programs. Medicare beneficiaries who lose coverage through no fault of their own remain without the guaranteed protections this bill offered.

for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate

for.name: John D. Rockefeller IV

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after referral; it received no markup, no vote, and no floor consideration before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: The record shows too little activity to read a partisan split: a Republican sponsor, a Democratic co-introducer, and a mixed three-person cosponsor list, with no votes ever taken.

industries.note: The bill forces them to sell policies to applicants regardless of health status, without health-based pricing or pre-existing-condition exclusions, eliminating their ability to screen out the costliest customers. Their gain from avoiding this is the beneficiary's loss of access to affordable coverage.

Plans must conduct consumer satisfaction surveys and pay assessments toward the consumer information program, and must accept back enrollees displaced when plans exit or end contracts. The requirement to disclose satisfaction data also subjects them to public comparison.

industries.industry: Nonprofit consumer organizations and state agencies
industries.note: They would receive federal grants to prepare and distribute clear, standardized comparisons of Medigap policies and Medicare plans for beneficiaries.
